content.title: About
content.content: Butter in stick form (usually 200 g) is a solid block of pure butter packaged in a convenient rectangular shape. It is made from cow’s milk cream that has been churned into a smooth, creamy mass. The butter has a characteristic milky aroma, a gentle taste and a soft texture suitable for cooking as well as spreading.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally butter was divided into “soft” and “hard” – the stick belongs to the soft category because it slices easily.
In European culinary schools a stick is often used as a precise measure of butter (approximately 1 Tbsp ≈ 14 g).
Butter typically contains about 80 % fat, with the remaining 20 % being water and milk proteins.
Stored in the refrigerator, a butter stick stays fresh for up to 3 weeks; in the freezer it can last up to 6 months.
In some countries (e.g., Japan) butter sticks are sold in individual salted or herb‑flavored packages.

items.title: Source of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Butter is rich in vitamins A, D, E and K2, which support vision, immunity, skin health and bone metabolism.

items.title: Contains conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)
items.content: CLA may help maintain normal blood sugar levels and has antioxidant properties.

items.title: Supports gut health
items.content: Small amounts of short‑chain fatty acids in butter can promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The fats in butter are quickly absorbed, providing sustained satiety.

items.title: Improves nutrient absorption
items.content: The fatty matrix of butter enhances the absorption of other fat‑soluble nutrients in a meal.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake of saturated fat may raise LDL‑cholesterol, so moderation is recommended.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Butter contains trace amounts of lactose; people with severe intolerance should limit consumption.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein present in butter.

items.title: Oxidation if stored improperly
items.content: When kept at high temperatures butter can become rancid, affecting flavor and aroma.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: A butter stick is easy to slice for spreading on bread, adding to sauces, baking, or sautéing vegetables and meat. It can be melted for flavorful dressings or incorporated into dough for a softer crumb.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store butter in the refrigerator in its original wrapper or an airtight container. For longer storage (over 1 month) it can be frozen, wrapped tightly in plastic. Before use, check the smell – rancid butter has a sharp, unpleasant odor.
